summary:
We developed SAR Atlas, an interactive 3D globe that lets users explore how Earth’s surface changes using radar imagery from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission. Users can search for a location, compare dated radar images side by side, and play sequences of real satellite observations across 12 study sites. These sites include the Chókwè floodplain in Mozambique, farmland in Punjab, and glaciers in Greenland.

SAR Atlas addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by making it easier to see where radar observations changed over time and investigate what might explain those changes. The app brings in nearby event records from NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey to give users context for what they see. Because radar can collect imagery at night and through clouds, it can reveal surface conditions when optical imagery is limited. SAR Atlas gives students, educators, and the public a way to explore these observations and understand what the evidence can tell them.
details:
SAR Atlas is an interactive 3D globe that helps people investigate how Earth’s surface changes using NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations. Users can search for a city, enter coordinates, or click the globe to explore available imagery. The app includes 12 study sites across six continents, with three dated observations per site. Users can compare images side by side or play and scrub through the actual satellite acquisitions. A closer look at Houston and Galveston Bay lets users switch between HH and HV radar polarizations and see how water, vegetation, and built-up areas appear in each.

We made the atlas interactive because a radar image is easier to interpret when you have something to compare it with and a question to investigate. Six guided investigations give users a starting point. For example, they can look for changes along the Limpopo River floodplain near Chókwè, Mozambique, then check nearby event records for context. The app shows the dates, distances, and sources for nearby reports so users can judge how relevant they are. A nearby event can suggest an explanation, and confirming the cause requires additional evidence.

We built the browser app with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and used MapLibre GL JS to render the globe. We used Python scripts to package the app and its data. The atlas draws on NASA’s Global Imagery Browse Services for worldwide radar imagery, the Alaska Satellite Facility for NISAR acquisition records, and NASA EONET and the U.S. Geological Survey for event context.

Our team considered gaps in satellite coverage, differences between radar acquisitions, and how much data a browser needs to load. We kept observation dates visible, bundled compressed previews for the study sites, and removed a year-long comparison option where the available data could not support it. We also label visual comparisons so users know when they would need calibrated radar data to measure a change. Our goal is to give students, educators, and the public a way to work with real satellite observations, ask their own questions, and understand how much the evidence supports their conclusions.
